text: Freed from its floor, the pound fell.
By the end of 1992, it was around 2.45 Deutschmarks,
roughly 17% below the rate Britain had promised.
Against the dollar, it slid from about 1.85 to about 1.52.
Soros and his fund made about a billion dollars,
and a hedge fund manager almost nobody outside finance had heard of
got a new name, the man who broke the Bank of England.
And Britain? Spending reserves isn't the same as losing them. The real loss came from buying
pounds at the old price and watching them fall. When Treasury papers were finally released
in 2005, the best estimate of the cost was 3.3 billion pounds, about 57 pounds
for every man, woman, and child in the country.
I didn't spend 57 pounds. No, you were the 57 pounds.
The political bill was bigger. Just before the crisis, the governing conservatives were level with Labour in one poll, at 38 each.
By late November, Gallup had them at 29 against Labour's 52.
In 1997, Labour won by a majority of 178 seats.
Britain wasn't alone, either. Major later told Parliament that no system could have survived an attack on that scale.
In Sweden, he said, overnight rates had hit around 500%.
Across that crisis, the Bundesbank alone was forced to spend about 65 billion Deutschmarks
propping up other people's currencies.
A few days after the crash, in Washington, Lamont joked that his wife had heard him
singing in the bath.
He later said he was misreported.
The voters weren't singing.
By May 1993, Lamont was out of the Treasury.
